story: Joan Miró wrote an original surrealist poem and collaborated with publisher Louis Broder to produce a suite pairing his handwritten verses with lithographs, originally planned for release in 1967 [sothebys.com, pamono.com]. After printing the initial run, Miró and Broder discovered that a defect in the paper factory had caused an alteration of the colors [pamono.com]. Because the original lithographic plates had already been erased before the flaw was detected, the entire first edition had to be abandoned [christies.com, pamono.com]. Miró was forced to create an entirely new series of plates from scratch, delaying the project's final publication until 1971 [christies.com, pamono.com].

Art dealer Léonce Rosenberg originally initiated this collaborative project between painter Juan Gris and poet Pierre Reverdy during World War I, with sources dating its start to 1915, 1916, or 1917. The original plan paired one of Gris's plates with each of Reverdy's twenty poems, but work halted when Gris died of kidney failure in 1927 at age forty, leaving only eleven lithographs finished. Nearly thirty years after Gris's death, the publisher Tériade revived the stalled undertaking alongside Reverdy. The resulting book was finally published in 1955 containing the twenty poems accompanied by Gris's completed prints as a tribute to the late artist.

Sigmund Freud published his final book, *Moses and Monotheism*, in 1939, arguing that Moses was born into Egyptian nobility rather than Hebrew heritage. Decades later, Salvador Dalí illustrated the text by drawing directly onto massive gold plates with a diamond-tipped stylus. The resulting engravings were printed in color on lambskin. Dalí paired Freud’s historical psychoanalysis with his own nonsensical foreword, baffling readers with bizarre references to Confucius and the Perpignan train station.

work: Le Lézard aux plumes d’or (The Lizard with Golden Feathers)
story: In 1967, Joan Miró created a suite of lithographs to illustrate his own poem, *Le Lézard aux plumes d’or*, published by Louis Broder. Mid-way through production, Miró and Broder discovered that defects in the paper were chemically reacting with and deteriorating the printed colors. Because the original lithographic plates had already been erased, the prints could not simply be run again, leading the artist to reject and destroy the edition. Miró was forced to restart the artwork and execute a new series of plates, finally publishing the completed book in 1971.

Around 1916, art dealer Léonce Rosenberg brought poet Pierre Reverdy and painter Juan Gris together to create *Au Soleil du Plafond*, originally planning an illustration by Gris for each of Reverdy's twenty poems. Work halted when Gris died prematurely of kidney failure in 1927 at age forty; while some accounts state Gris had already completed eleven lithographs before his death, others note he left behind original gouaches that the printer Mourlot Frères later translated into lithographs. Nearly thirty years after the project stalled, publisher Tériade revived it alongside Reverdy. Reverdy reconceived the publication as a posthumous tribute to his late friend, issuing the final volume in 1955.

Sigmund Freud wrote *Moses and Monotheism* on the origins of monotheistic tradition just before his death in 1939. In 1974, Salvador Dalí created *Moïse et le Monothéisme*, entering into a dialogue with Freud through a graphic suite based on the text. Dalí issued the project as a complete book of graphic works accompanied by a bas-relief sculpture.

In 1974, Salvador Dalí produced a series of illustrations to interpret Sigmund Freud’s final 1939 text, *Moses and Monotheism*. He collaborated across traditional disciplines to produce the work as a *livre d'artiste*, integrating typography, text, and visual art into an autonomous book format displayed at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston. While records describe the edition as being printed on sheepskin, others identify the support material as lambskin or parchment. Dalí engraved plates directly with a diamond stylus and paired Freud's study of religious history with his own visual imagery and an idiosyncratic foreword.
